items.explanation: Montgomery showed that disciplined nonviolence could fill jails, boycott businesses, and win in court without firing a shot. College students in Greensboro, Nashville, and Atlanta copied the model in 1960, sitting politely at whites-only lunch counters, accepting arrest, and training in nonviolent resistance. The sit-in movement was Montgomery's tactical heir. Option B is wrong because the late-1960s uprisings abandoned nonviolence. Option C is wrong because Black Power emphasized self-determination and often rejected integrationist nonviolence. Option D is wrong because filibusters were a Southern segregationist weapon in Congress, not a protest tactic.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the 1960 sit-ins copied Montgomery's disciplined nonviolent mass action.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the urban uprisings rejected nonviolence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Black Power diverged from integrationist nonviolence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: filibusters were used by segregationists in Congress.

options: (A) The 1960 student sit-ins at segregated Southern lunch counters.
(B) The urban uprisings of the late 1960s.
(C) The Black Power movement's separatism.
(D) Southern filibusters against civil rights bills conducted on the floor of the United States Senate.
items.stem: The Montgomery bus boycott's strategy of disciplined nonviolent mass protest was most directly echoed by which of the following?

items.explanation: Long before Montgomery, the NAACP had pursued equality through the courts, chipping at segregation case by case until Brown v. Board of Education (1954) declared school segregation unconstitutional. Browder v. Gayle, which ended bus segregation in Montgomery, extended that same legal strategy to public transportation. Option A is wrong because the Klan used terror against the movement. Option B is wrong because colonization sought to send Black Americans to Africa, a nineteenth-century idea. Option C is wrong because loyalty investigations targeted suspected communists, not segregation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the Klan terrorized civil rights supporters.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: colonization proposed removing Black Americans from the country.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: loyalty programs targeted suspected communists.
option_explanations.D: Correct: the court victory continued the NAACP's legal campaign.

options: (A) The Ku Klux Klan's campaign of intimidation.
(B) The nineteenth-century colonization movement.
(C) The federal loyalty investigations of suspected communists.
(D) The NAACP's decades-long legal challenge to segregation.
items.stem: The boycott's victory in the federal courts (Browder v. Gayle, 1956) continued which longer-running civil rights strategy?

items.explanation: Friedan interviewed suburban housewives who had educations, comfortable homes, and healthy children yet felt restless and empty. She named that restlessness the feminine mystique: a culture that told women fulfillment came only through husband, children, and home, while closing off careers and public life. Option A is wrong because Friedan argued domesticity denied women professional fulfillment. Option C is wrong because she described political marginalization, not dominance. Option D is wrong because she criticized the narrowness of domestic life, not family itself.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Friedan argued domesticity blocked professional fulfillment.
option_explanations.B: Correct: she described educated women feeling empty and cut off from wider purpose.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: she portrayed women as politically sidelined, not dominant.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: she criticized the narrowness of the homemaker role, not family life itself.

options: (A) Economically independent and professionally fulfilled.
(B) Unfulfilled, cut off from purposes beyond housework.
(C) Politically dominant in national elections.
(D) Determined to abandon their families entirely.

items.explanation: Friedan's book helped launch the modern women's movement: she co-founded the National Organization for Women in 1966, and activists pressed the government to enforce the new ban on sex discrimination in employment found in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Equal employment opportunity became the movement's first great legal battleground. Option A is wrong because the Equal Rights Amendment passed Congress but was never ratified. Option B is wrong because women's suffrage had been won in 1920, decades earlier. Option D is wrong because no 1965 decision struck down all abortion restrictions; Griswold (1965) concerned contraception, and Roe v. Wade came in 1973.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the ERA was never ratified.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: women won the vote in 1920.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Title VII (1964) banned sex discrimination in employment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the 1965 Griswold decision concerned contraception, not abortion.

options: (A) Ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment.
(B) Women's suffrage in federal elections.
(C) Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning sex discrimination in employment.
(D) A 1965 Supreme Court decision striking down all abortion restrictions nationwide, establishing a constitutional right to abortion.

items.explanation: The cult of domesticity was the ideal itself: it taught that respectable women belonged in the home as wives and mothers, which reinforced rather than challenged traditional roles. Each of the other developments pushed against that ideal. Option B is wrong as an answer because wartime factory work proved women could do industrial jobs. Option C is wrong as an answer because the New Woman pursued college, careers, and public life. Option D is wrong as an answer because the suffrage victory brought women into electoral politics.

option_explanations.A: Correct as the exception: the cult of domesticity reinforced traditional roles.
option_explanations.B: Not the exception: wartime factory work challenged domestic expectations.
option_explanations.C: Not the exception: the New Woman pursued education and public life.
option_explanations.D: Not the exception: suffrage brought women into politics.

items.explanation: After Reconstruction, Southern states imposed poll taxes alongside literacy tests and other devices to evade the Fifteenth Amendment. The taxes fell hardest on poor Black sharecroppers, who could not afford to pay simply for the right to vote. The Twenty-fourth Amendment, pushed by the civil rights movement, removed that barrier in federal elections. Option A is wrong because the voting age was lowered by the Twenty-sixth Amendment in 1971. Option C is wrong because women's suffrage was secured by the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Option D is wrong because literacy tests were suspended by the Voting Rights Act of 1965, not this amendment.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the voting age was lowered by the Twenty-sixth Amendment.
option_explanations.B: Correct: the amendment targeted poll taxes used to disfranchise Black voters.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: women's suffrage came via the Nineteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: literacy tests were addressed by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

options: (A) Lower the voting age to eighteen.
(B) Remove the financial barrier Southern states used to keep Black citizens from voting.
(C) Guarantee women's right to vote.
(D) Abolish literacy tests for voters in federal and state elections throughout the Southern states.

items.explanation: The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments promised freedom, citizenship, and the vote to Black Americans. Southern states answered with a new system of control: poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses that stripped Black men of the vote without mentioning race. The poll tax was part of the Jim Crow counterrevolution against Reconstruction. Option A is wrong because the Nineteenth Amendment came in 1920, after poll taxes were entrenched. Option B is wrong because the Seventeenth Amendment concerned senators, not voting qualifications. Option C is wrong because poll taxes predated the New Deal by decades.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: poll taxes predated women's suffrage.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Seventeenth Amendment addressed Senate elections.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: poll taxes were adopted decades before the New Deal.
option_explanations.D: Correct: Southern states used poll taxes to evade the Reconstruction amendments.

items.explanation: Reagan argued that decades of growing federal programs, taxes, and regulation had smothered enterprise and freedom. The line summed up the New Right's conviction that government itself, swollen since the New Deal, was the source of stagflation and national decline rather than its cure. Option A is wrong because Reagan sought to shrink Great Society programs, not expand them. Option B is wrong because he pushed to cut taxes, especially on high earners. Option D is wrong because he presented the New Deal era as the start of the problem.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Reagan aimed to shrink Great Society programs.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: he championed tax cuts, not tax increases.
option_explanations.C: Correct: he blamed federal growth since the New Deal for economic and civic decline.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: he treated the New Deal as the beginning of the problem.

options: (A) The Great Society's antipoverty and civil rights programs should be expanded to finish the work the New Deal had begun.
(B) Taxes on the wealthy should be raised.
(C) Federal growth since the New Deal had damaged the economy and individual liberty.
(D) The New Deal deserved praise for saving capitalism.
items.stem: Reagan's famous line expressed which of the following convictions?
items.stimulus: "In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem." Source: Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, 1981 (public domain).

items.explanation: Reagan united three strands of the rising right: economic conservatives who wanted tax cuts and deregulation, evangelical Christians mobilized over abortion and school prayer, and anti-communists who demanded a military buildup against the Soviet Union. Together they formed the New Right coalition that realigned American politics. Option B is wrong because unions mostly backed Democrats and Reagan famously broke the PATCO strike. Option C is wrong because civil rights groups opposed his domestic cuts. Option D is wrong because liberal academics were among his sharpest critics.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the New Right combined economic, religious, and anti-communist conservatives.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: unions largely opposed Reagan, who broke the PATCO strike.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: civil rights organizations opposed his domestic agenda.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: liberal academics were among his critics.

options: (A) Economic conservatives, evangelical Christians, and staunch anti-communists united against Soviet power.
(B) Labor union leaders and industrial workers who had traditionally supported Democratic candidates since the New Deal era.
(C) Civil rights organizations.
(D) Liberal academics and journalists.

items.explanation: By 1980 the American economy suffered stagflation: prices rose rapidly while growth stalled and unemployment stayed high, a combination that baffled the Keynesian remedies of the postwar era. Reagan's audience would have recognized the ills as the inflation and economic drift of the Carter years. Option A is wrong because the 1929 crash belonged to a different era. Option B is wrong because wartime controls were long gone. Option C is wrong because the technology bubble burst in 2000, two decades later.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the 1929 crash was half a century earlier.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: wartime price controls were long past.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the tech bubble collapsed around 2000.
option_explanations.D: Correct: stagflation combined high inflation with high unemployment.

options: (A) The stock market crash of 1929.
(B) Wartime price controls and rationing imposed on the American economy during World War II.
(C) The collapse of the technology bubble.
(D) Stagflation: high inflation occurring alongside high unemployment.
